## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |
| Likely gap | Vagueness. Autonomy without written scope reads as management failure, not freedom |
| Add | Precision — documented decision rights, thresholds, escalation triggers. More documentation produces more autonomy here, counter-intuitively |
| Drop | Motivational framing and aspirational language; actively corrosive of credibility |
| Failure mode | Formal structural objection: "not properly specified, and it touches co-determination" — and they will be right on both counts |
| 60-day indicator | Existence of a signed, unit-level decision-rights schedule; count of decisions taken against it |
| Watch item | **Works councils** — Betriebsrat, ondernemingsraad, Nordic union structures. Changes to appraisal criteria, working methods and monitoring are frequently co-determination matters. Engage as co-designers, not as clearance (§10.2) |
| Quiet opportunity | This cluster will build the best delegation architecture in the network. We would suggest letting it lead the design and having other regions borrow from it, rather than the reverse — a small reversal of the usual flow that would itself say something useful about the initiative |

### Card C — Latin Europe (FR, IT, ES, PT, GR)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Moderate-to-high authority distance; direct on substance, relationship-mediated in form; individual attribution with strong reputational weight; moderate ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Relational legitimacy. It must come from a leader people are personally loyal to, or it is noise from the centre |
| Add | Public named conferral (§4.

[NEW REQUEST]

A competitor that switched abruptly lost a fifth of its installed base.

Plan the business-model transition to subscription revenue. Define the offer structure and migration incentives for existing license holders, the pricing that balances trough depth against adoption, the sales compensation redesign, and the financial communication plan that keeps investors and the board committed through the trough.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

### 0. Threshold finding: there is no output to review

### 1. What the missing deliverable must contain (specification for the re-run)

The request names four mandatory workstreams. A passing output addresses all four *quantitatively*, with an integrated model — not four essays.

**A. Offer structure and migration incentives**
- Must open with the legal reality the prompt's framing obscures: **a perpetual licence is a granted, irrevocable right.** You cannot revoke it. You can only (i) stop selling new perpetuals, (ii) change maintenance/support pricing and terms on renewal, (iii) withhold new functionality from the perpetual entitlement, and (iv) make the subscription materially more valuable. Any plan that assumes forced migration is legally defective and will produce the competitor's 20% loss. Flag this explicitly.
- Requires a **migration ladder**, not a single offer: maintenance-price escalation on the perpetual line (e.g., +8–12%/yr, pre-announced 24 months ahead), maintenance credit toward subscription, new-feature and cloud-service exclusivity to subscription, term-licence as a bridge product for customers with capex-only budgets or air-gapped deployments.
- Must segment: enterprise/negotiated vs. mid-market vs. long-tail; on-maintenance vs. lapsed-maintenance (the lapsed base is the *cheapest* conversion pool and is usually missed); regulated/on-prem customers who structurally cannot go SaaS.
- Must define **grandfathering with an expiry**: a price-protected conversion window (e.g., 18–24 months) after which conversion economics worsen. Open-ended offers produce no urgency and a permanent two-population estate.

**B. Pricing and trough depth**
- Must show the arithmetic explicitly: a $X perpetual + 20% maintenance converts to $Y ACV; the multiple $Y/(perpetual + maintenance) determines both **payback period per converted customer** and **trough depth**. Roughly: pricing subscription at ~35–40% of perpetual ASP + maintenance yields ~2.5–3 year revenue-neutral payback per customer and a 2–3 year GAAP trough.
- Must present a **sensitivity table** across at least three variables: conversion price ratio, conversion pace (% of base per year), and churn-at-conversion. Report trough depth (peak-to-trough GAAP revenue), trough duration, cumulative FCF drawdown, and the year of ARR crossover.
- Must distinguish **GAAP revenue trough from cash trough**. These diverge sharply if you offer annual-prepay subscriptions, and the difference is the single most useful thing to tell the board. Annual prepay with a discount (~8–10%) is the standard lever for shrinking the *cash* trough while accepting the GAAP one.
- Must address **ASC 606 mechanics**: term licences with on-prem delivery recognise a licence component upfront (which can be used deliberately to soften the trough, at the cost of metric cleanliness); true SaaS is fully ratable. State the accounting position and the deferred-revenue/RPO consequences, and note the balance-sheet optics of a shrinking maintenance deferred-revenue balance.

**C. Sales compensation redesign**
- Must solve the actual conflict: reps paid on TCV/upfront will defend the perpetual motion, and a naive switch to ACV quotas cuts realised earnings 50–70% in year one, triggering the top-quartile attrition that kills the transition.
- Required components: quota redenomination into ACV/net-new-ARR; **multi-year TCV multipliers or accelerators on subscription** to restore earnings parity; SPIFFs on *conversion* of installed base (a distinct motion from new logo); an **earnings guarantee / draw for 4–6 quarters** for top performers; explicit de-rating of perpetual quota credit on a published schedule (e.g., 100% → 70% → 40% → 0 across three years) so the trend is legible and reps self-select forward.
- Must separate roles: a dedicated **installed-base conversion team** (renewal/CSM-led, lower cost-of-sale) rather than asking enterprise hunters to farm. Must state the cost-of-sale implication and the resulting change in S&M as % of revenue during the trough.
- Must name the retention risk quantitatively and budget for it. Sales comp redesign cost belongs in the trough model, not outside it.

**D. Investor and board communication**
- Must specify a **metric handover**: stop guiding on GAAP revenue/EPS; introduce ARR, net revenue retention, cRPO/RPO, subscription mix %, conversion cohort rates, and FCF. Do this *at least one quarter before* the trough begins — changing the scoreboard after the score drops is read as concealment.
- Must include a **pre-announced trough**: publish the expected depth, duration and crossover year at an analyst day, with the model assumptions. Investors punish surprises, not declines. The Adobe/Autodesk precedent is the argument; use it and cite the mechanics, not the mythology.
- Must handle the board separately from the street: a milestone/tripwire schedule (conversion pace, NRR floor, churn-at-conversion ceiling, sales attrition ceiling) with **pre-agreed responses** if a tripwire trips — including what would constitute grounds to slow, not abandon, the transition. Pre-committing the failure test prevents mid-trough panic reversals, which are the dominant failure mode.
- Must address capital structure: buyback authorisation to signal confidence and absorb the multiple compression, covenant headroom under a shrinking recognised-revenue profile, and management incentive plans re-based on ARR/FCF rather than EPS. Leaving executive comp on EPS while asking for a three-year EPS trough is self-sabotage.
- Should address the **competitor's 20% loss** directly as a named counter-example, with an explicit statement of which of their choices this plan avoids (abrupt cut-off, no term bridge, no price protection, no lapsed-maintenance amnesty).

---

### 2. Structural requirements

- **One integrated model, one set of numbers.** The four workstreams must reconcile: pricing ratio drives trough depth drives comp affordability drives investor guidance. Four independently-reasoned sections that don't tie is the most likely failure of the re-run.
- **A phased timeline with dates and gates** (typically: 6-month prep, ~30-month conversion window, perpetual end-of-sale date announced ~12–18 months ahead).
- **An explicit decision request** to the board: end-of-sale date, conversion price ratio, comp guarantee budget, and the guidance-metric switch date.
- **Illustrative but internally consistent numbers.** No revenue baseline was given; the re-run should state a clearly-labelled illustrative baseline (e.g., $400M revenue, 60% perpetual/40% maintenance) and carry it through, rather than writing qualitatively.

---

### 3. Anti-patterns to reject in the re-run

- Treating this as a pricing exercise. It is a **cash-flow, incentive and credibility** exercise; pricing is one of four dials.
- "Offer both and let customers choose" with no forcing function. This produces a decade-long dual estate and no multiple re-rating.
- Assuming conversion is voluntary and frictionless while also assuming a 2–3 year trough. Those assumptions are inconsistent.
- Silence on the customers who *cannot* convert (regulated, air-gapped, capex-only). They need a permanent term-licence answer, not a migration incentive.
- Adopting the prior document's hedged, consultative-apologetic tone. The board needs a decision memo with numbers, not a discussion paper.

---

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
